# Cycle s and Decoded Quantum Interferometry

**Abstract**

Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) reduces optimization problems with two-variable constraints to decoding cycle codes. For one such problem, namely MaxCut, prior work showed that DQI achieves a nontrivial satisfaction fraction guarantee only on linear-girth graphs, for which MaxCut is classically easy. However, these no-go results rely on minimum distance assumptions that do not represent true decodability thresholds for common noise channels, thus underestimating actual DQI performance. To estimate the true performance, we derive DQI satisfaction guarantees in the presence of imperfect decoding for fixed instances and generalize prior results for random instances. We then study homological cycle codes over arbitrary finite fields, and show that minimum-weight decoding is NP-hard for every field of size _q\>_2, in contrast with known results for binary cycle codes. On the Linial–Simkin ensemble of regular graphs with logarithmic girth, we prove maximum-likelihood recovery bounds and a strong converse for a family of non-uniform additive noise channels. Moreover, LP decoders provide polynomial-time recovery of a positive fraction of randomly located errors with arbitrary values. These results allow us to prove upper and lower bounds on the approximate optima achievable by DQI when restricted to classical decoders. These bounds rule out quantum advantage in the regimes we analyze but also identify a family of regular Max-_k_-Cut instances on which DQI efficiently achieves a nontrivial satisfaction fraction guarantee.

## 1 Introduction

In many commonly studied optimization problems, one is given a list of constraints, each of which involves only a small subset of the decision variables, and seeks to maximize the number of constraints satisfied. Some paradigmatic examples of this are the Max-3-SAT and MaxCut optimization problems over binary variables, both of which are NP-hard. Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) is a quantum algorithm that uses a quantum Fourier transform to reduce such optimization problems to decoding problems for LDPC codes \[Jor+25\]. The quality of the approximate optimum found by DQI is determined by the number of symbol-flip errors that can be decoded. The existence of efficient decoding algorithms for LDPC codes at high error rates raises the tantalizing possibility of quantum advantage on the corresponding optimization problems. However, the competing classical optimization heuristics are quite powerful, and such quantum advantage has not yet been realized.

The clearest examples of quantum advantage via DQI known to date arise from cases where DQI reduces an optimization problem to decoding an algebraic code \[Jor+25; GJ25\]. In \[CLZ22\], a quantum Fourier transform is used to reduce a constraint satisfaction problem to a decoding problem for codes defined by a dense, algebraically unstructured parity check matrix, which was then solved using a quantum decoding algorithm, yielding a potential quantum advantage. Subsequent work \[KOW25\] gave a classical counterattack eliminating quantum advantage in many parameter regimes, but whether the algorithm of \[CLZ22\] can retain advantage in some domain is an unresolved question.

Here we investigate the application of DQI to optimization problems in which each constraint contains exactly two variables. Such problems are reduced by DQI to problems of decoding from codes in which each symbol is contained in exactly two parity checks. s over a binary alphabet with this property are known as _cycle codes_, and they behave very differently from codes whose variables participate in at least three parity checks, i.e., conventional LDPC codes. Specifically, we consider DQI applied to Max-LINSAT, defined as follows.

**Definition 1** (Max-LINSAT)**.** _Let_ \(B\in\unknown_q^{m\times n}\) _and let_ \(C_i\subseteq\unknown_q\) _for i_=1_,...,m. Max-LINSAT asks for_ \(\mathbf{x}\in\unknown_q^n\) _satisfying as many as possible of the constraints_ \(\sum_jB_{ij}x_j\in C_i\).

When every row has two nonzero entries, the problem is Max-2-LINSAT. Over F_<sub>q</sub>_, the constraints \(x_v-x_u\neq 0\) give Max-_k_-Cut for prime powers _k=q_. Setting _q_=2 gives MaxCut.

Cycle codes are directly associated with graphs, where each edge represents a symbol in the codeword, and the vertices at its two ends are the two parity checks in which it is contained. For regular graph families of fixed degree at least three, cycle codes have minimum distance at most logarithmic in block size. Thus, one cannot guarantee recovery from all error patterns with more than logarithmically many bit flips. Nevertheless, for suitable growing-girth ensembles described below, a linear number of independent random bit flips can be corrected with high probability \[DZ97; NZ16\]. Furthermore, for cycle codes, the nearest codeword problem is solvable exactly in polynomial time \[EJ73\]. In contrast, for general LDPC codes, the nearest codeword problem is NP- hard \[XH07\], although belief propagation solves the problem efficiently given a sufficient promise on the rate of bit flip errors \[RU01\].

Because cycle codes behave so differently from other LDPC codes, the performance of DQI on optimization problems in which each constraint contains two variables must be analyzed separately from the case in which each constraint contains three or more variables. In particular, efficient classical algorithms attain the optimal-decoding threshold of cycle codes. This is helpful to DQI, as the number of constraints it can satisfy in the original optimization problem increases with the<tbc>

<tbc>number of errors that can be corrected in the decoding problem. However, in \[Jor+25\], for max-2- LINSAT over F<sub>2</sub> with random target sets, it was shown that this advantage is outweighed by the lower optimal-decoding threshold of cycle codes, relative to the LDPC ensembles in which bits are contained in three or more parity checks.

Here, we investigate a natural next question: what happens when we no longer restrict our attention to a binary alphabet? DQI reduces Max-2-LINSAT to decoding a non-binary generalization of cycle codes. Prior to the present work, these were poorly understood compared to binary cycle codes. One of the main contributions of this paper is to initiate the study of _q_-ary cycle codes (hereafter simply "cycle codes"). We resolve several foundational questions about the decoding complexity and reliability of _homological_ cycle codes, in which the two nonzero coefficients in a column of the parity check matrix sum to zero. These results are summarized in  1. A polynomial-time linear programming (LP) decoder also has a provably positive error-rate guarantee on this ensemble (Corollary 2), although we do not prove that it attains the ML threshold.

** 1: Binary versus nonbinary homological cycle codes.** Here the block length is _m_ and the number of parity checks is _n_. The graph degree is _D_, and therefore _m=Dn/_2. For independent uniformly distributed nonzero errors, maximum-likelihood (ML) decoding limits concern whole-word error averaged over the Linial-Simkin ensemble of Definition 4, as \(n\rightarrow\infty\) at fixed degree _D_, fixed finite field size _q_, fixed Linial-Simkin girth parameter _c_, and fixed error probability \(p\in(0,1-1/q)\).

If we choose the graph defining a binary or nonbinary homological cycle code uniformly at random from all simple _D_-regular graphs, with \(D\ge 3\) fixed, the resulting ensemble has no positive reliability threshold. That is, for every fixed 0_\<p\<_1-1_/q_, independently changing each symbol with probability _p_, uniformly among the other _q_-1 values, and then using a maximum-likelihood decoder leaves a whole-word error probability, averaged over the graph, that is bounded away from zero as the block size grows. The reason is that short cycles persist with nonvanishing probability, and a fixed pattern of errors on a short cycle can give a competing codeword higher likelihood regardless of the errors elsewhere in the graph. In the binary case, this follows by combining the classical cycle-error criterion \[NZ16, §2.2\] with the short-cycle statistics of random regular graphs \[MWW04\]. We prove the corresponding error-floor bound over every finite field in §3.2, Theorem 3.

Therefore, rather than considering uniformly random _D_-regular graphs without restriction, we consider the _Linial-Simkin random greedy ensemble_ \[LS20\]. Specifically, let _G_ have _n_ labelled vertices and _m=Dn/_2 edges. Fix \(D\ge 3\), a girth coefficient \(c\in(0,1)\), and _n_ even, and put

\(g(n):=\mathrm{max}\{3,\lfloor c\mathrm{log}_{D-1}n\rfloor\}.\) (1)

The Linial-Simkin ensemble consists of simple, connected graphs with girth at least _g(n_). The ensemble is most easily defined by an algorithm for sampling from it, which we do in Definition 4. Throughout the threshold analysis, the block length tends to infinity first, with _D_, _q_, _c_, and _p_ fixed; only afterward do we vary _D_ and _q_.

Given a graph _G_, and a corresponding homological code _C<sub>G</sub>_, we consider the success probability of a maximum-likelihood decoder given a codeword from _C<sub>G</sub>_ in which each symbol has been independently corrupted with probability _p_. Specifically, a corrupted symbol is replaced with another of the _q_-1 elements of F_<sub>q</sub>_ uniformly at random. Let \(P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{ML}(G,p)\) denote the probability that a maximum-likelihood decoder fails to recover the correct original codeword. Let E_<sub>G</sub>_ denote the expectation with _G_ drawn from the Linial-Simkin ensemble. Define the reliability threshold by

\(\delta_\mathrm{rel}(D,q):=\mathrm{sup}\big\{p\in[0,1-1/q]:\unknown_GP_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{ML}(G,p)\rightarrow 0\text{as}n\rightarrow\infty\big\}.\) (2)

The notation \(\delta_\mathrm{rel}(D,q)\) suppresses the fixed girth coefficient _c_.  1 compares two complementary guarantees: _reliable recovery_, where the ML word-error probability tends to zero, and _asymptotically certain failure_, where it tends to one.

For _q=o(D_<sup>2/3</sup>), including fixed _q_ as \(D\rightarrow\infty\), the success and failure bounds are asymptotically equal to (_q_-1)/(4_D_<sup>2</sup>). The explicit finite-parameter statement uses the simple-cycle value<tbc>

\(\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,q):=\frac{q-1}{(D-1)\big(\sqrt{D+q-2}+\sqrt{D-2}\big)^2}.\) (3)

<tbc>Whenever \(q/D^{2/3}\le 1/32\), Theorem 5 gives

\(\unknown_GP_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{ML}(G,p)\rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
0, & 0<p<(1-16q/D^{2/3})\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,q), \\
1, & \delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,q)<p<1-1/q.
\end{array}\right.\) (4)

In fact, \(\unknown_GP_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{ML}(G,p)\rightarrow 1\) for \(\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,q)<p<1-1/q\) holds at every fixed \(D\ge 3\) and _q_. In the binary case \(\unknown_GP_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{ML}(G,p)\) is known to converge to a perfect step function with transition at \(\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,2)\) for every \(D\ge 3\) \[DZ97; NZ16\].

<tbc>Two of the most prominent examples of optimization problems in which each constraint contains exactly two variables are MaxCut and Max-_k_-Cut. For MaxCut, a semicircle law restricted to half the minimum distance cannot give a constant improvement over random guessing \[Par25\]. On the other hand, despite the low minimum distance, suitable ensembles of regular graphs permit reliable decoding of a linear number of random errors \[DZ97; NZ16\]. This discrepancy suggests that DQI could be performant on such ensembles. To realize these gains, one must move beyond an understanding of DQI in terms of worst-case decoding guarantees, as dictated by the code minimum distance. Within classical error correction, code performance is more reliably captured by _noise thresholds_ with respect to a given communication channel, which only require success with high probability. Analogously, one should expect DQI to perform reliably out to thresholds corresponding to the noise that the algorithm artificially generates via the weights **w**.

In §2 we prove a version of the semicircle law that applies to fixed Max-LINSAT target sets and accounts for decoding errors. Our fixed-target semicircle law, Theorem 1, together with our LP decoding theorem Theorem 6 and Corollary 2, proves that DQI can, in polynomial time, achieve a satisfaction fraction on MaxCut and Max-_k_-Cut that is asymptotically bounded away from random guessing, but not sufficient to achieve quantum advantage over known classical algorithms. Our algorithmic conclusions are summarized in  2.

## 2 Decoded Quantum Interferometry with imperfect decoding

Let \(B\in\unknown_q^{m\times n}\) have rows **b**_<sub>i</sub>_, and fix target sets **C**=(_C_<sub>1</sub>_,...,C<sub>m</sub>_) with \(C_i\subseteq\unknown_q\) and |_C<sub>i</sub>_|=_r_, where 0_\<r\<q_. The Max-LINSAT objective is<tbc>

\(s(\mathbf{x}):=\sum_{i=1}^m\unknown_{C_i}(\mathbf{b}_i\cdot\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{x}\in\unknown_q^n.\) (5)

<tbc>Writing \(\rho=r/q\), define the centered, normalized target indicators<tbc>

\(g_i(x):=\frac{\unknown_{C_i}(x)-\rho}{\sqrt{q\rho(1-\rho)}}.\) (6)

<tbc>For \(q=\ell_0^\nu\) with \(\ell_0\) prime, use the additive character<tbc>

\(\chi_q(t):=\mathrm{exp}\left(\frac{2\pi i}{\ell_0}\mathrm{Tr}_{\unknown_q/\unknown_{\ell_0}}(t)\right),\mathrm{Tr}_{\unknown_q/\unknown_{\ell_0}}(t):=\sum_{j=0}^{\nu-1}t^{\ell_0^j}.\) (7)

<tbc>It satisfies \(\chi_q(s+t)=\chi_q(s)\chi_q(t)\), \(\overline{\chi_q(t)}=\chi_q(-t)\), and<tbc>

\(\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\unknown_q^d}\chi_q(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{x})=q^d\unknown_\mathbf{0}(\mathbf{a}).\) (8)

<tbc>Thus the Fourier transform with entries \((\mathsf{F}_q)_{a,x}=\chi_q(ax)/\sqrt{q}\) is unitary. Set<tbc>

\(\widetilde{g}_i(a):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{q}}\sum_{x\in\unknown_q}\chi_q(ax)g_i(x),\) (9)

<tbc>so that \(\widetilde{g}_i(0)=0\) and \(\sum_a|\widetilde{g}_i(a)|^2=1\). For an error word \(\mathbf{y}\in\unknown_q^m\), define

\(\widetilde{g}_\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y}):=\prod_{i:y_i\neq 0}\widetilde{g}_i(y_i),\) (10)

with the empty product equal to one.

DQI prepares an error state specified by a normalized amplitude vector \(\mathbf{w}=(w_0,\dots,w_m)\in\unknown^{m+1}\):<tbc>

\(|\Gamma\rangle:=\sum_{\mathbf{y}\in\unknown_q^m}\phi_\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y})|\mathbf{y}\rangle,\phi_\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y}):=\frac{w_{|\mathbf{y}|}}{\sqrt{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{|\mathbf{y}|}}}\widetilde{g}_\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y}).\) (11)

<tbc>Since<tbc>

\(\sum_{|\mathbf{y}|=k}|\widetilde{g}_\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y})|^2=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{k},\) (12)

<tbc>this state is normalized and assigns probability |_w<sub>k</sub>_|<sup>2</sup> to errors of weight _k_. For state preparation, let \(|D_k^m\rangle\propto\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^m:|\mathbf{z}|=k}|\mathbf{z}\rangle\) be the normalized Dicke state. Applying \(U=\otimes_iU_i\) to \(|\mathbf{w}\rangle:=\sum_kw_k|D_k^m\rangle\) gives \(|\Gamma\rangle\), where _U<sub>i</sub>_ are the isometries into \(\unknown^q\) given by<tbc>

\(U_i|0\rangle=|0\rangle,U_i|1\rangle=\sum_{a\in\unknown_q^\times}\widetilde{g}_i(a)|a\rangle.\) (13)

The decoder acts on syndromes of \(C^\perp=\mathrm{ker}B^T\). We assume that \(D:\mathrm{im}B^T\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_q^m\) is deterministic and syndrome-consistent:<tbc>

\(B^TD(\mathbf{s})=\mathbf{s}\text{for all}\mathbf{s}\in\mathrm{im}B^T.\) (14)

<tbc>Computing the syndrome produces

\(\sum_\mathbf{y}\phi_\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y})|\mathbf{y}\rangle|B^T\mathbf{y}\rangle.\) (15)

A reversible implementation of _D_ then subtracts _D(B<sup>T</sup>_**y**) from the error register. Postselecting this register on \(|\mathbf{0}\rangle\) retains exactly the decoder’s success set

\(\mathcal{S}:=\{\mathbf{y}:D(B^T\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{y}\},\mathcal{F}:=\mathbb{F}_q^m\backslash\mathcal{S}.\) (16)

Because _B<sup>T</sup>_ is injective on S, the resulting normalized syndrome state is

\(|\widetilde{P}_\mathcal{S}\rangle\propto\sum_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{S}}\phi_\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y})|B^T\mathbf{y}\rangle.\) (17)

The algorithm applies \((\mathsf{F}_q^\dagger)^{\otimes n}\) and measures in the computational basis to obtain an assignment **X**. All expected satisfaction fractions below are conditioned on successful postselection. The analysis applies to any implementation of the state preparation and reversible decoder described above.

For each target _C<sub>i</sub>_, put

\(\theta_i(a):=|\widetilde{g}_i(a)|^2=\frac{\left|\sum_{t\in C_i}\chi_q(at)\right|^2}{r(q-r)}.\) (18)

These probabilities satisfy \(\theta_i(a)=\theta_i(-a)\). Let _P<sub>k</sub>_ be the error distribution obtained by choosing _k_ coordinates uniformly and drawing their nonzero values independently from the corresponding \(\theta_i\). This is the DQI error distribution conditioned on weight _k_.

**Theorem 1** (Semicircle law for fixed targets)**.** _Let_ \(\ell\le m\) _be a positive integer, and let_ \(\varepsilon\in[0,1)\)_. Suppose that, for every_ \(0\le k\le\ell\),

\(\mathrm{Pr}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_k}\left[D(B^T\mathbf{Y}')=\mathbf{Y}'\text{\textit{for every}}\mathbf{Y}'\text{\textit{with}}|\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{Y}'|\le 1\right]\ge 1-\varepsilon.\) (19)

_Let_ \(f_\ell^*\) _be the largest value of_ E\[_s_(**X**)_/m_| _successful postselection_\] _over all normalized shell-amplitude vectors_ **w**=(_w_<sub>0</sub>_,...,w<sub>m</sub>)<sup>T</sup> satisfying w<sub>k</sub>_=0 _for_ \(k>\ell\)_. Put_ \(\rho:=r/q\) _and_ \(p_\ell:=\mathrm{min}\{\ell/m,1-\rho\}\)_, and define_

\(F_\rho(p):=\left(\sqrt{\rho(1-p)}+\sqrt{(1-\rho)p}\right)^2.\) (20)

_Then_

\(f_\ell^*\ge(1-\varepsilon)\left(F_\rho(p_\ell)-\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\right)-\frac{\sqrt{(q-1)\rho(1-\rho)}\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon},f_\ell^*\le(1-\varepsilon)F_\rho(p_\ell)+\varepsilon+\frac{\sqrt{(q-1)\rho(1-\rho)}\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}.\text{(21)}\)

_Every such normalized shell-amplitude vector has postselection probability at least_ \(1-\varepsilon\).

_Proof._ We first derive the error-space representation of satisfaction for arbitrary fixed targets and amplitudes. Define

\(\mathsf{S}:=\sum_\mathbf{x}s(\mathbf{x})|\mathbf{x}\rangle\langle\mathbf{x}|,\mathsf{S}_\mathrm{err}:=\sum_{i=1}^m\Pi_i,\Pi_i:=\sum_{t\in C_i}|t\rangle\langle t|,\) (22)

where \(\Pi_i\) acts on coordinate _i_ of the error register. A tilde denotes conjugation by the Fourier transform on all coordinates. For \(X_\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}\rangle=|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{z}\rangle\), Fourier expansion gives

\(\kappa_i(a):=\frac{1}{q}\sum_{t\in C_i}\chi_q(-at),\) (23)

\(\widetilde{\mathsf{S}}=\sum_{i,a}\kappa_i(a)X_{-a\mathbf{b}_i},\) (24)

\(\widetilde{\mathsf{S}}_\mathrm{err}=\sum_{i,a}\kappa_i(a)X_{-a\mathbf{e}_i}.\) (25)

Here and below, \(i\in[m]\) and \(a\in\unknown_q\) unless otherwise indicated. In particular, \(0\unknown\widetilde{\mathsf{S}}_\mathrm{err}\unknown mI\).

Let V be the shell isometry \(\mathsf{Vw}:=U\sum_kw_k|D_k^m\rangle=|\Gamma\rangle\). The local span of the uniform vector \(|u\rangle=q^{-1/2}\sum_x|x\rangle\) and \(|g_i\rangle=\sum_xg_i(x)|x\rangle\) is invariant under \(\Pi_i\), because both vectors are constant on _C<sub>i</sub>_ and on its complement. Using Eqs. (6) and (13) gives

\(U_i^\dagger\widetilde{\Pi}_iU_i=\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
\rho & \sqrt{\rho(1-\rho)} \\
\sqrt{\rho(1-\rho)} & 1-\rho
\end{array}\right].\) (26)

This matrix is independent of _i_, so its sum over coordinates preserves the symmetric qubit subspace. Thus ranV is invariant under \(\widetilde{\mathsf{S}}_\mathrm{err}\). The restriction \(T_\rho=\mathsf{V}^\dagger\widetilde{\mathsf{S}}_\mathrm{err}\mathsf{V}\) is tridiagonal, with entries

\((T_\rho)_{kk}=m\rho+(1-2\rho)k,(T_\rho)_{k,k+1}=(T_\rho)_{k+1,k}=\sqrt{\rho(1-\rho)(k+1)(m-k)}.\) (27)

Next consider decoding. Let \(\Pi_\mathcal{S}\) project onto the success set from (16), and define

\(Z_\mathbf{C}:=\sum_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{S}}|\phi_\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y})|^2.\) (28)

For _Z_**<sub>C</sub>**_\>_0, the normalized successful error and output states are

\(|\Gamma_\mathcal{S}\rangle:=Z_\mathbf{C}^{-1/2}\Pi_\mathcal{S}|\Gamma\rangle,\) (29)

\(|\widetilde{P}_\mathcal{S}\rangle:=Z_\mathbf{C}^{-1/2}\sum_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{S}}\phi_\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y})|B^T\mathbf{y}\rangle,|P_\mathcal{S}\rangle:=(\mathsf{F}_q^\dagger)^{\otimes n}|\widetilde{P}_\mathcal{S}\rangle.\) (30)

## 3 Decoding cycle codes over general fields

Let _G_ be an undirected, simple graph with vertex set _V_ and edge set _E_. To define a homological cycle code from _G_, fix an orientation of each edge _e_, and a nonzero weight \(a_e\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times\). Let \(B^T\in\mathbb{F}_q^{V\times E}\) be the weighted incidence matrix in which column _e_, oriented from _u_ to _v_, has two nonzero entries: _a<sub>e</sub>_ in row _v_ and -_a<sub>e</sub>_ in row _u_. The cycle code \(C^\perp\) is the code whose parity check matrix is _B<sup>T</sup>_.

\(C^\perp:=ker(B^T)=\{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbb{F}_q^E:B^T\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{0}\}\) (57)

One can visualize homological cycle codes as incompressible flows on graph _G_. Observe that a vector \(\mathbf{d}\in\mathbb{F}_q^E\) satisfies _B<sup>T</sup>_**d**=**0** exactly when the weighted sum of the edge values at every vertex vanishes in F_<sub>q</sub>_. That is, the net flux into each vertex is zero. Linearity of the code can be understood by noting that sums of incompressible flows are also incompressible. The name "cycle code" reflects the fact that this space is spanned by the signed circulation vectors of the simple cycles of _G_.

For homological cycle codes, the minimum distance \(d_{min}(C^\perp)\) is fixed by the geometry of the underlying graph. Since \(C^\perp\) is linear, _d_<sub>min</sub> is exactly the smallest weight of a nonzero codeword. Because every nonzero codeword **d** is a valid flow, its associated subgraph supp**d** has no vertex of degree one, since zero-flux would be violated at that vertex. Hence each nonzero codeword contains a cycle of _G_, implying \(d_{min}\ge g(G)\), where _g(G_) is the girth. Conversely, any single cycle carries a valid flow supported on exactly its edges. By considering the flow along the shortest cycle, we have the complementary bound \(d_{min}\le g(G)\). Thus, _d_<sub>min</sub>=_g_ for cycle codes, independent of _q_. Because of this, cycle codes on the bounded-degree graph families most useful for decoding cannot have large distance. The Moore bound \[Big93\] forces the girth of a _D_-regular graph, for any fixed _D_, to grow at most logarithmically in the number of vertices, and hence so does the distance. Remarkably, however, families of cycle codes often are still able to correct, with high probability, a number of errors that grows linearly with block size, thus demonstrating a significant gap between worst-case and probabilistic error correction capabilities.

### 3.1 NP-hardness of minimum-weight decoding

An important task in coding theory (and practice) is determining a nearest codeword **d** to some given string **y**, which may be thought of as the output of some noisy communication channel.

**Definition 2** (Nearest word Problem)**.** _Given a block code_ \(C^\perp\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^m\) _and a string_ \(\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{F}_q^m\)_, the nearest codeword problem is to find the codeword_ \(\mathbf{d}\in C^\perp\) _nearest to_ **y** _in Hamming distance._

When \(C^\perp\) is linear, this problem is equivalent to minimum-weight syndrome decoding with respect to its parity check matrix _B<sup>T</sup>_: writing **s**=_B<sup>T</sup>_**y** for the syndrome, finding the nearest codeword **d** is equivalent to finding a minimum-weight \(\mathbf{e}\in\mathbb{F}_q^m\) satisfying _B<sup>T</sup>_**e**=**s**, via the relation **e**=**y**-**d**. We now prove the NP-hardness of nearest codeword in this syndrome-decoding formulation for<tbc>

cycle codes on alphabets of size three or more. This stands in contrast to cycle codes on the binary alphabet, for which nearest-codeword decoding is known to be solvable in polynomial time by a T-join decoding algorithm \[EJ73\].

**Theorem 2.** _For every fixed finite field_ F_<sub>q</sub> with q\>_2_, the following decision problem is NP- complete. Given a homological cycle code with parity-check matrix B<sup>T</sup>, a syndrome_ **s**_, and an integer_ \(w\ge 0\)_, decide whether there exists_ \(\mathbf{e}\in\mathbb{F}_q^m\) _with B<sup>T</sup>_**e**=**s** _and_ \(|\mathbf{e}|\le w\)_. Consequently, nearest-codeword decoding is NP-hard for these codes._

_Proof._ Membership in NP follows by checking the syndrome and weight. For hardness, we reduce from perfect three-dimensional matching \[GJ09\]: given disjoint sets _U_<sub>1</sub>_,U_<sub>2</sub>_,U_<sub>3</sub>, each of size _k_, and a set of triples \(\mathcal{T}\subseteq U_1\times U_2\times U_3\), decide whether there exists a subset of _k_ triples from T that covers every element exactly once.

Choose \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times\) with \(\alpha+\beta\neq 0\) (possible because _q\>_2) and put \(\gamma=-\alpha-\beta\). All three are nonzero, their sum is zero, and no nonempty proper subcollection has sum zero. This holds also in characteristic two.

Construct a bipartite incidence graph with vertex set \(V=P\sqcup L\), with "element vertices" \(P=U_1\sqcup U_2\sqcup U_3\), and "triplet vertices" _L_=T . Join each triplet vertex \(T\in\mathcal{T}\) to its three elements, orienting the edges from _T_ to those elements, and take _B<sup>T</sup>_ to be its oriented incidence matrix. Define a syndrome \(\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{F}_q^V\) by assigning entries in _U_<sub>1</sub>_,U_<sub>2</sub>_,U_<sub>3</sub> values \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\), respectively, and entries in T value 0. Set _w_=3_k_.

An exact cover yields an error \(\mathbf{e}\in\mathbb{F}_q^E\) of weight 3_k_ by assigning the three edges of each chosen triple the respective values \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). The triplet-vertex equations hold because their sum is zero. Conversely, all 3_k_ element syndromes are nonzero, so an error of weight at most 3_k_ has exactly one nonzero edge at each element. That edge’s value is forced to equal the element syndrome. At a triplet vertex, the selected incident values are a subcollection of \(\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}\), which sums to zero only if none or all three are selected. The selected triples therefore form an exact cover. This reduction gives a simple graph.

## 3.2 Decoding thresholds for even symbol-wise additive channels

We now study ML whole-word decoding for the homological cycle codes on _D_-regular graphs. Throughout this subsection, _B<sup>T</sup>_ is an oriented incidence matrix, _n_=|_V(G_)|, and _m_=|_E(G_)|=_Dn/_2. For a weighted homological incidence matrix, these results apply after multiplying each error coordinate by its incidence weight, provided the transformed errors have the common distribution specified below. Uniform nonzero replacement is preserved by this normalization.

We consider additive channels in which each symbol is corrupted by adding an error \(a\in\mathbb{F}_q\), whose distribution is as follows. Fix a probability distribution \(\theta\) on \(\mathbb{F}_q^\times\) which is _even_, i.e., \(\theta(a)=\theta(-a)\), and write

\(\nu_p(0)=1-p,\nu_p(a)=p\theta(a)(a\neq 0)\) (58)

We refer to \(\theta\) as the _replacement distribution_. An important special case, when all symbols are equally likely to occur given a flip, is the _q_-ary symmetric channel.

**Definition 3** (_q_-ary symmetric channel)**.** _The q-ary symmetric channel (qSC) has uniform replacement_ \(\theta(a)=1/(q-1)\) _for all_ \(a\neq 0\) _and_ \(0\le p\le 1-q^{-1}\).

Let \(\mathbf{E}\in\unknown_q^m\) denote the random variable representing the full error vector obtained by drawing _m_ independent errors from \(\nu_p\). Let \(P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{ML}(G,p,\theta)\) be the minimum whole-word error probability in recovering **E** from _B<sup>T</sup>_**E**, and put \(P_\mathrm{S}^\mathrm{ML}=1-P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{ML}\). Thus

\(P_\mathrm{S}^\mathrm{ML}(G,p,\theta)=\sum_{\mathbf{s}\in\unknown_q^V}\mathrm{max}_{\mathbf{e}\in\unknown_q^E}\prod_{j=1}^m\nu_p(e_j).\) (59)

This is also ML codeword success for a uniformly distributed transmitted codeword, and it is independent of the choice among equal-likelihood maximizers. For uniform \(\theta\), we retain the notation \(P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{ML}(G,p)\). For _p\<_1-_q_<sup>-1</sup>, the likelihood of an error decreases with Hamming weight, so ML syndrome decoding is minimum-weight decoding. Its worst-case hardness for _q\>_2 does not preclude efficient recovery at lower noise levels, as the LP guarantees below demonstrate.

From the Moore bound \[Big93\], the girth for _D_-regular graphs can be at most logarithmic in terms of the number of vertices, as given by

\(g(G)\le 2\mathrm{log}_{D-1}(n)+O(1).\) (60)

However, many graphs such as random regular graphs contain short cycles whose distribution is Poissonian \[MWW04\]. The presence of these short cycles hurts the decoding performance, leading to a word error rate bounded away from zero.

**Theorem 3** (Error floor from short cycles)**.** _Fix_ \(D\ge 3\)_, a finite field_ \(\unknown_q\)_, an even replacement distribution_ \(\theta\)_, and_ 0_\<p\<_1/2_. If G<sub>n</sub> is uniform among simple D-regular graphs on n labeled vertices, then_

\(\mathrm{liminf}_{n\rightarrow\infty}\unknown_{G_n}P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{ML}(G_n,p,\theta)\ge(p\theta_\mathrm{max})^3\left(1-\mathrm{exp}\left[-\frac{(D-1)^3}{6}\right]\right)>0,\) (61)

_where_ \(\theta_\mathrm{max}:=\mathrm{max}_a\theta(a)\)_. The limit is through n\>D with Dn even. The same statement holds after conditioning on connectedness._

_Proof._ Whenever _G<sub>n</sub>_ contains a triangle, select one deterministically and orient its unit circulation **f**. Choose \(a\neq 0\) with \(\theta(a)=\theta_\mathrm{max}\). With probability \((p\theta_\mathrm{max})^3\), the error equals _a_**f** on the triangle, because \(\theta\) is even. Subtracting this circulation leaves the syndrome and all other coordinates unchanged, while replacing three entries of probability \(p\theta_\mathrm{max}\) by zero entries of probability \(1-p>p\theta_\mathrm{max}\). Thus the resulting error is strictly more likely, and every ML decoder fails on the original error. Therefore

\(P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{ML}(G_n,p,\theta)\ge(p\theta_\mathrm{max})^3\mathbf{1}_{\{G_n\text{contains a triangle}\}}.\) (62)

The triangle count converges to a Poisson random variable with mean (_D_-1)<sup>3</sup>/6 \[MWW04; Joh15\]. Averaging the preceding inequality and taking the lower limit proves (61). The probability of connectedness tends to one \[Bol01\], so conditioning on connectedness leaves the same limit.

Excluding cycles only up to any fixed length still leaves a positive error floor, by the joint Poisson limit for the remaining fixed cycle lengths \[MWW04; Joh15\]. We therefore employ an ensemble with girth growing logarithmically.

**Definition 4** (Linial-Simkin ensemble)**.** _Fix_ \(D\ge 3\), \(c\in(0,1)\)_, and even n. Set_<tbc>

\(g(n):=max\{3,\lfloor clog_{D-1}n\rfloor\}.\) (63)

<tbc>_Begin with a fixed Hamilton cycle H on_ \[_n_\]_. When the current minimum degree is k_-1_\<D, choose uniformly an unordered pair of degree-(k_-1) _vertices at current graph distance at least g(n_)-1_, and add the edge between them. Abort if no such pair exists; otherwise continue until the graph is D-regular. A completed degree-increment round adds a perfect matching, so a successful run has the form_

\(G=H\cup M_1\cup\cdots\cup M_{D-2}.\) (64)

_Let_ L_<sub>n,D,c</sub> be the output probability distribution conditioned on successful completion._

Every successful output of the Linial-Simkin process is simple, connected, and has girth at least _g(n_). The completion probability tends to one by \[LS20, Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 2.1\], while the uniform choice of admissible pairs is part of the definition.

We now turn to the ML decoding properties of the Linial-Simkin graphs. The key point is that the syndrome determines the error only modulo the cycle space:

\(B^T\mathbf{e}=B^T\mathbf{e}'\Longleftrightarrow\mathbf{e}-\mathbf{e}'\in kerB^T.\) (65)

Thus every nonzero circulation \(\mathbf{f}\in kerB^T\) gives a possible competitor **E**-**f** to the true error **E**. ML decoding succeeds precisely when the true error is the most likely element of its syndrome coset. Consequently, the basic obstruction to ML decoding is a circulation \(\mathbf{f}\neq 0\) for which **E**-**f** is at least as likely as **E**. For a fixed circulation **f**, this pairwise confusion probability is controlled by the Bhattacharyya overlap between the probability distribution over noise vectors and its coordinatewise translate. Indeed, writing

\(L(\mathbf{e}):=\prod_{j=1}^m\nu_p(e_j),\) (66)

the elementary inequality<tbc>

\(\mathbf{1}_{\{L(\mathbf{e}-\mathbf{f})\ge L(\mathbf{e})\}}L(\mathbf{e})\le\sqrt{L(\mathbf{e})L(\mathbf{e}-\mathbf{f})}\) (67)

<tbc>gives

\(Pr\{L(\mathbf{E}-\mathbf{f})\ge L(\mathbf{E})\}\le\sum_{\mathbf{e}\in\mathbb{F}_q^E}\sqrt{L(\mathbf{e})L(\mathbf{e}-\mathbf{f})}=\prod_{j:f_j\neq 0}\sum_{z\in\mathbb{F}_q}\sqrt{\nu_p(z)\nu_p(z-f_j)}.\) (68)

Thus the worst single-coordinate overlap controls the pairwise ML error probability for every competing circulation, with a cost exponential in the support size of that circulation. This is the same channel parameter that appears in standard pairwise ML bounds for group codes on symmetric channels \[Com08, §2.5\].

The competing objects here are cycles and, more generally, circulations. A _D_-regular graph has approximately \((D-1)^\ell\) possible non-backtracking closed walks of length \(\ell\), while each nonzero coordinate of a competing circulation contributes a factor at most \(Z_\theta(p)\) to the pairwise overlap, where<tbc>

\(Z_\theta(p):=max_{a\neq 0}\sum_{z\in\mathbb{F}_q}\sqrt{\nu_p(z)\nu_p(z-a)},\) (69)

or equivalently

\(Z_\theta(p)=\mathrm{max}_{a\neq 0}\left\{2\sqrt{p(1-p)\theta(a)}+p\sum_{z\notin\{0,a\}}\sqrt{\theta(z)\theta(z-a)}\right\},\) (70)

which is non-decreasing for \(0\le p\le 1/2\). Hence, the natural branching condition is

\((D-1)Z_\theta(p).\) (71)

When this quantity is below one, the total contribution of long cycle-like competitors is summable, and reliability can hold. When it is above one, the graph contains exponentially many sufficiently independent cycle competitors, and their aggregate likelihood overwhelms the true error, giving a strong converse. This motivates the following definition.

\(\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,\theta):=\mathrm{inf}\{p\in[0,1/2]:(D-1)Z_\theta(p)\ge 1\},\) (72)

with value 1/2 if this set is empty.

We now prove the condition under which the whole-word decoding error rate goes to unity or vanishes. Define the _reliability threshold_

\(\delta_\mathrm{rel}(D,\theta):=\mathrm{sup}\left\{p\in[0,1/2]:\mathrm{lim}_{n\rightarrow\infty}\unknown_{G\sim\mathcal{L}_{n,D,c}}P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{ML}(G,p,\theta)=0\right\}.\) (73)

The limit is taken with _n_ even and other parameters fixed. For uniform \(\theta\), write \(\delta_\mathrm{rel}(D,q)\).

**Theorem 4** (ML strong converse)**.** _Fix_ \(D\ge 3\)_, a finite field_ \(\unknown_q\), \(c\in(0,1)\)_, and an even replacement distribution_ \(\theta\)_. For the Linial-Simkin ensemble and independent errors with distribution (58),_

\((D-1)Z_\theta(p)>1\Longrightarrow\unknown_GP_\mathrm{S}^\mathrm{ML}(G,p,\theta)\rightarrow 0,0<p\le 1/2.\) (74)

_In particular,_ \(\delta_\mathrm{rel}(D,\theta)\le\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,\theta)\)_. For uniform replacement, the same strong converse holds throughout_ \(\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,q)<p\le 1-q^{-1}\).

**Theorem 5** (Small-alphabet ML reliability)**.** _Fix_ \(c\in(0,1)\) _and an even replacement distribution_ \(\theta\) _on_ \(\unknown_q^\times\)_. For the Linial-Simkin ensemble, if_ \(\gamma=q/D^{2/3}\le 1/32\)_, then_

\((1-16\gamma)\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,\theta)\le\delta_\mathrm{rel}(D,\theta)\le\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,\theta).\) (75)

_Throughout the lower interval, a minimum-Hamming-weight syndrome decoder recovers the errors with probability tending to one, as does the optimal ML decoder. As_ \(D\rightarrow\infty\)_, uniformly over even_ \(\theta\) _and finite fields with q=o(D_<sup>2/3</sup>),

\(\frac{\delta_\mathrm{rel}(D,\theta)}{\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,\theta)}\rightarrow 1,\delta_\mathrm{rel}(D,\theta)=\frac{1+o(1)}{4\theta_\mathrm{max}D^2}.\) (76)

Both proofs are in Appendix A. The recovery proof also shows that, with probability tending to one, every word differing from the error in at most one coordinate is uniquely recovered by the minimum-weight decoder; see Lemma 6.

For uniform replacement, Eqs. (69) and (72) reduce to

\(Z_q(p)=2\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{q-1}}+\frac{q-2}{q-1}p,\) (77)

\(\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,q)=\frac{q-1}{(D-1)(\sqrt{D+q-2}+\sqrt{D-2})^2}.\) (78)

Since \(Z_q(1/2)>1/2\ge 1/(D-1)\), this crossing lies below 1/2; the full-range strong converse therefore justifies the notation \(\delta_\mathrm{rel}(D,q)\) used above. Thus Theorem 5 gives \(\delta_\mathrm{rel}(D,q)\sim(q-1)/(4D^2)\) when _q=o(D_<sup>2/3</sup>). For _q_=2, the reliability endpoint is exact at every \(D\ge 3\):

\(\delta_\mathrm{rel}(D,2)=\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,2)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{(D-1)^2}}\right).\) (79)

## 3.3 Decoding with Linear Programming

Although minimum-weight decoding is NP-hard for _q\>_2, a polynomial-time decoder can still recover from a positive fraction of randomly located symbol errors. We establish this for the standard nonbinary local-polytope LP decoder \[Fla+09\] on the Linial-Simkin ensemble. The recovery bound uses only the graph’s degree and girth but is independent of the alphabet size.

### 3.3.1 The decoder

Let _H=B<sup>T</sup>_, write _h<sub>ve</sub>=H<sub>ve</sub>_, and let \(\partial v\) be the edges incident to _v_. Given a syndrome \(\mathbf{s}\in\mathrm{im}H\), define the local constraint set

\(\mathcal{C}_v(s_v):=\left\{(b_e)_{e\in\partial v}\in\unknown_q^{\partial v}:\sum_{e\in\partial v}h_{ve}b_e=s_v\right\}.\) (80)

Instead of choosing a single error value on each edge _e_, the LP assigns a probability _x<sub>e,a</sub>_ to each possible value \(a\in\unknown_q\). These real-valued variables are called _symbol marginals_; write **x** for the vector of all such variables. At each vertex _v_, the LP also chooses a probability distribution \(\lambda_{v,\mathbf{b}}\) over the assignments in C_<sub>v</sub>(s<sub>v</sub>_). The two local distributions involving an edge must give the same marginal probabilities for its value. The constraints are

\(x_{e,a}\ge 0,\sum_{a\in\unknown_q}x_{e,a}=1,\lambda_{v,\mathbf{b}}\ge 0,\sum_{\mathbf{b}\in\mathcal{C}_v(s_v)}\lambda_{v,\mathbf{b}}=1,x_{e,a}=\sum_{\mathbf{b}\in\mathcal{C}_v(s_v)b_e=a}\lambda_{v,\mathbf{b}}(v\in V,e\in\partial v,a\in\unknown_q).\text{(81)}\)

The local distributions need not come from a joint distribution on complete words satisfying all checks. The LP minimizes the relaxed Hamming weight

\(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{e\in E}(1-x_{e,0}).\) (82)

We call the marginal vector **x** _integral_ when every _x<sub>e,a</sub>_ is either zero or one, and _fractional_ otherwise. Every syndrome-consistent word **y** gives an integral feasible point _x<sub>e,a</sub>_=**1**{_a=y<sub>e</sub>_}, with objective value |**y**|. Conversely, normalization and local consistency ensure that every integral feasible marginal vector represents a syndrome-consistent word. An integral optimum therefore gives a minimum-weight word with the specified syndrome, and hence an ML correction on the _q_SC \[Fla+09\].

If the LP has several optimal solutions, select one using a fixed deterministic tie-breaking rule. If the selected symbol marginals are integral, output the corresponding word; otherwise declare failure. Let \(P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{LP}(G,p)\) be the probability of either a declared failure or an incorrect output when each position is corrupted independently with probability _p_; the nonzero values may have any distribution. The recovery condition below guarantees that the true error has the unique optimal marginal vector, so recovery under this condition is independent of the tie-breaking rule.

An equivalent formulation uses a directed trellis whose state records the running sum in each check. Unit flows through this trellis represent probability distributions on satisfying local assignments. Equating their symbol marginals gives an LP with _O(mq_<sup>2</sup>) variables and constraints, solvable in polynomial time; see Appendix B for more details. The LP decoder has a failure probability which we characterize in the following theorem:

## 3.3.2 A positive error-rate guarantee

**Theorem 6** (Finite-graph LP reliability)**.** _Let G be a simple graph with m edges, maximum degree at most_ \(D\ge 3\)_, and girth g<sub>G</sub>. Consider its homological cycle code over_ F_<sub>q</sub> with each position corrupted independently with probability_ 0_\<p\<_1/2 _and arbitrary nonzero error values. For every integer_ \(1\le h<g_G\)_, the probability that the LP decoder declares failure or returns an incorrect word satisfies_

\(P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{LP}(G,p)\le 2m(D-1)^{h-1}\left[2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\right]^h.\) (83)

_The same bound holds when exactly_ \(t\le pm\) _positions are chosen uniformly without replacement and assigned arbitrary nonzero error values._

The proof in Appendix B shows that the true error is the unique LP optimum whenever every simple path of _h_ edges contains fewer than _h/_2 corrupted positions. Counting paths and applying a binomial or hypergeometric tail bound gives (83). Related path-based conditions for binary LP decoding appear in \[EH12\]. Requiring fewer than _h/_2-1 corrupted positions on each path also guarantees recovery after every one-coordinate change. The failure probability for this stronger condition is at most

\(2m(D-1)^{h-1}\frac{1-p}{p}\left[2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\right]^h.\) (84)

The extra factor is independent of block length.

On the Linial-Simkin ensemble, the girth grows logarithmically with _n_. Choosing _h_ just below the girth in (83) gives the following positive error-rate guarantee.

**Corollary 2** (Linear-error LP recovery on the Linial-Simkin ensemble)**.** _Fix_ \(D\ge 3\)_, a finite field_ F_<sub>q</sub>, and_ \(c\in(0,1)\)_. Define the certified rate_

\(p_\mathrm{LP}^\mathrm{cert}(D,c):=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\sqrt{1-(D-1)^{-2(1+1/c)}}\right)>0.\) (85)

_For every fixed_ 0_\<p\<p_<sub>LP</sub><sup>cert</sup>(_D,c), there is a constant_ \(\kappa>0\) _such that_

\(sup_{G\in supp\mathcal{L}_{n,D,c}}P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{LP}(G,p)=O_{D,c,p}(n^{-\kappa})\rightarrow 0.\) (86)

_The same conclusion holds for a uniformly random support of exactly_ \(\lfloor pm\rfloor\) _nonzero errors, where m=Dn/_2_. Both conclusions also hold for the probability of failure on the error or any one- coordinate modification, uniformly over the nonzero error values._

_Proof._ Put \(R=2(D-1)\sqrt{p(1-p)}\). The strict inequality in the hypothesis is equivalent to _R\<(D_-1)<sup>-1_/c_</sup>. Every successful output has girth at least _g(n_) from (63). For sufficiently large _n_, set _h=g(n_)-1=_c_log<sub>_D_-1</sub>_n+O_(1) in (83). Uniformly over these graphs,

\(P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{LP}(G,p)\le\frac{nD}{D-1}R^h=O_{D,c,p}\big(n^{1+clog_{D-1}R}\big).\) (87)

Take \(\kappa=-1-clog_{D-1}R>0\). The fixed-weight statement follows from the same finite-graph bound, and the one-coordinate statement follows from (84).

The bound holds uniformly over every graph produced by the ensemble. The certified rate is independent of _q_, because the proof uses only the error locations and discards information about the nonzero error values. It can be smaller than the actual LP threshold and does not establish the factor-(_q_-1) improvement proved for ML decoding. The guarantee applies to random error locations; but it does not imply recovery from every error pattern of linear weight. The numerical experiments in the next subsection compare the noise rates tolerated by LP decoding with the ML decoding threshold at accessible block lengths.

## 4 DQI performance and classical comparison

In this concluding section, we combine the analysis of §2 with the decoding results of §3 to study DQI performance on problems dual, in the Regev sense, to decoding homological cycle codes. In particular, we focus on the Linial-Simkin ensemble and DQI instantiated by LP decoding in superposition. The following corollary provides the direct connection needed to make our performance claims below.

**Corollary 3** (DQI from cycle-code reliability)**.** _Fix_ \(D\ge 3\)_, a finite field_ F_<sub>q</sub>, and_ \(c\in(0,1)\)_. Consider Max-2-LINSAT instances on the LS ensemble G_∼L_<sub>n,D,c</sub> (Definition 4) with target sets of common size r such that the corresponding noise channels all have a shared error distribution_ \(\theta\)_. Let_ \(\rho=r/q\)_. Call a cutoff rate_ \(p\in[0,1/2]\) _reliable if there are syndrome decoders returning zero on the zero syndrome for which the failure probability in Theorem 1, with_ \(\ell=\lfloor pm\rfloor\)_, tends to zero in ensemble mean. Let_ \(F_{D,\theta,r}^\text{DQI}\) _be the supremum of the limiting expected satisfaction fractions obtained by optimizing the weights_ **w** _at reliable cutoff rates. Then_

\(F_{D,\theta,r}^\text{DQI}\le F_\rho(min\{\delta_\text{cyc}(D,\theta),1-\rho\}).\) (88)

_If_ \(\gamma=q/D^{2/3}\le 1/32\)_, then also_

\(F_{D,\theta,r}^\text{DQI}\ge F_\rho(min\{(1-16\gamma)\delta_\text{cyc}(D,\theta),1-\rho\}).\) (89)

_For q_=2_, the upper bound is attained for every_ \(D\ge 3\).

The bounds concern cutoffs for which decoding is asymptotically reliable. If \(\delta_\text{cyc}(D,\theta)<1/2\), the upper bound also excludes reliable cutoff rates above 1/2. This includes uniform replacement at every _D,q_.

_Proof._ At a reliable rate _p_, the optimized fraction converges in probability to \(F_\rho(min\{p,1-\rho\})\) by Theorem 1. It also converges in mean, because satisfaction fractions lie in \[0,1\]. If \(p>\delta_\text{cyc}(D,\theta)\), choose \(\delta_\text{cyc}(D,\theta)<p'<min\{p,1/2\}\). A binomial error count at rate \(p'\) is at most \(\lfloor pm\rfloor\) with probability tending to one. The assumed uniform shell recovery would therefore imply reliable channel decoding at \(p'\), contradicting Theorem 4. This proves (88).

Conversely, Theorem 5 and Lemma 6 give one-coordinate recovery for the lexicographically first minimum-weight decoder at every \(p'\le(1-16\gamma)\delta_\text{cyc}(D,\theta)\). For any smaller _p_, Lemma 7 transfers this guarantee to all shells through \(\lfloor pm\rfloor\). Apply Theorem 1 and let _p_ increase to the certified endpoint to obtain (89). For _q_=2, the binary recovery proof establishes the same property at every \(p'<\delta_\text{cyc}(D,2)\). Substitute (79) into \(F_{1/2}(p)=1/2+\sqrt{p(1-p)}\).

Note that the analysis of §2 requires a deterministic, syndrome-consistent output for every valid syndrome, whereas the LP decoder declares failure in certain scenarios. To make it a valid DQI decoder, we modify it as follows. When the LP declares failure, return a solution of _H_**y**=**s** found by Gaussian elimination, with free coordinates set to zero in a fixed order. This defines a polynomial-time map _D_LP with _D_LP(0)=0. The word-error probability of the resulting decoder is at most \(P_\mathrm{W}^\mathrm{LP}\), since declared failures were already counted as errors, so it inherits (86).

For a fixed-target DQI instance with \(\ell=\lfloor pm\rfloor\) and \(p<p_\mathrm{LP}^\mathrm{cert}\), the fixed-weight version makes the failure probability in Theorem 1 tend to zero, uniformly over weights through \(\ell\). Consequently the optimized satisfaction fraction tends to _F<sub>r/q</sub>_(min{_p,_1-_r/q_}) for arbitrary target sets of size _r_.

## 4.1 MaxCut and Max-_k_-Cut

Having established a firm connection between decoding LS cycle codes and DQI performance, we turn to our first application of interest: the well-known problem of MaxCut and its generalization, Max-_k_-Cut.

**Definition 5** (Max-_k_-Cut)**.** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be a simple graph. Max-k-Cut asks for an assignment_ \(\mathbf{x}:V\rightarrow[k]\) _maximizing the number of edges_ \(\{u,v\}\in E\) _with_ \(x_u\neq x_v\)_. The cut fraction is this number divided by m_=|_E|. MaxCut is Max-2-Cut._

As the name suggests, MaxCut admits a visualization as the number of edges "cut" by a bipartition of the vertices. More generally, Max-_k_-Cut can be understood as a vertex coloring problem in which, given a fixed number of colors _k_, one seeks to color the vertices to minimize the number of adjacent vertices with the same color.

Max-_k_-Cut is an instance of Max-2-LINSAT when _k=q_ is a prime power. We identify the labels with F_<sub>q</sub>_ and orient the edges. The constraints are \(x_v-x_u\in\unknown_q\backslash\{0\}\), so _B<sup>T</sup>_ is an oriented incidence matrix, _r=q_-1, and (18) gives \(\theta(a)=1/(q-1)\). Thus the semicircle formula is

\(b_q(p):=F_{(q-1)/q}(p)=\frac{\left(\sqrt{(q-1)(1-p)}+\sqrt{p}\right)^2}{q}.\) (90)

It increases from the random-assignment fraction (_q_-1)_/q_ to 1 on \(0\le p\le 1/q\).

Write \(F_{q,D}^\mathrm{DQI}\) for the optimal asymptotic cut fraction among the reliably decoded cutoff families of Corollary 3 on the Linial-Simkin ensemble. For this Max-_k_-Cut comparison, take _q\<D_, as in  3. Here \(\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,q)<1/(D-1)\le 1/q\). Substituting the ML decoding threshold bound (78) into the semicircle formula (90) gives<tbc>

\(F_{q,D}^\mathrm{DQI}\le U_q(D):=b_q\big(\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,q)\big).\) (91)

<tbc>For \(q/D^{2/3}\le 1/32\), the same corollary gives the lower bound \(b_q\big((1-16q/D^{2/3})\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,q)\big)\). Conse quently, for _q=o(D_<sup>2/3</sup>),

\(F_{q,D}^\mathrm{DQI}=\frac{q-1}{q}\left(1+\frac{1}{D-1}\right)+o(D^{-1}).\) (92)

For MaxCut, the exact binary threshold in (79) gives the exact reliable-decoding value

\(F_{2,D}^\mathrm{DQI}=\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,2)(1-\delta_\mathrm{cyc}(D,2))}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2(D-1)}.\) (93)

The polynomial-time LP decoder attains cut fractions approaching \(b_q\big(p_\mathrm{LP}^\mathrm{cert}(D,c)\big)\) by Corollary 2 and Theorem 1. For _q\>_2, the sharper lower bound above uses minimum-weight decoding, which is NP-hard in general.

We first compare DQI performance to the classical vector algorithm of Thompson, Parekh, and Marwaha (TPM) \[TPM22\], followed by Gaussian rounding \[FJ97\]. We observe that TPM gives a larger improvement at large degree on the same ensemble. As the girth grows, the inner product of adjacent unit vectors tends to \(\sigma_D=-2\sqrt{D-1}/D\). Assigning each vertex the label with largest inner product among _q_ independent standard Gaussian vectors gives the limiting expected cut fraction

\(T_q(D)=1-q\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}\phi_{\sigma_D}(x,y)\Phi_{\sigma_D}(x,y)^{q-1}dxdy,\sigma_D=-\frac{2\sqrt{D-1}}{D},\) (94)

where \(\phi_\sigma\) and \(\Phi_\sigma\) are the standard bivariate Gaussian density and distribution function with correlation \(\sigma\). The integral is the probability that one specified label wins at both endpoints. For _q_=2, \(T_2(D)=\mathrm{arccos}(\sigma_D)/\pi\). Expanding at zero correlation gives, with independent _Z<sub>a</sub>_∼N(0,1),

\(T_q(D)=\frac{q-1}{q}+\frac{\kappa_q}{\sqrt{D}}+O_q(D^{-1}),\kappa_q=\frac{2}{q-1}\left(\unknown\mathrm{max}_{1\le a\le q}Z_a\right)^2>0.\) (95)

This exceeds the _O<sub>q</sub>(D_<sup>-1</sup>) improvement of reliably decoded DQI at large _D_. The TPM limit also exceeds _U<sub>q</sub>(D_) at every parameter pair in  3.

Second, we compare DQI with simulated annealing (SA). We start each run from a uniformly random assignment and return the best assignment visited. A sweep visits every vertex, proposing a uniformly chosen different label and accepting it by the Metropolis rule, with energy equal to the number of unsatisfied constraints. The inverse temperature increases linearly between sweeps, with endpoints chosen on separate tuning instances. For Max-_k_-Cut, the same evaluation graphs are used for every field at a given degree; their sizes, girth, and sampling errors are given in  3.

<tbc> 3 presents a comparison of all three methods. SA gives the largest mean cut fraction in all 21 cases, exceeding the TPM limit by 0.94-6.98 percentage points and the DQI upper bound by 3.64-20.87 points. Seven cases yield perfect cuts on all 16 graphs. The theoretical entries are asymptotic; the SA entries are finite-size measurements. At every other step select a uniform available pair avoiding all endpoints of still-pending edges of _F_. For purposes of defining a probability measure, insert a forced edge even when it is unavailable; call such a trajectory _invalid_. Forced endpoints are either protected or already matched, so no unforced edge ever touches _V(F_). Even on invalid trajectories the graph is simple and has maximum degree _D_, and the unforced choices exist because at least \(m-2s\gg n^c\) outside vertices remain free.

This recovery guarantee also holds simultaneously after every single-coordinate modification of the error. ## Appendix B Proof of the LP-decoding guarantee

This appendix proves Theorem 6 using the direct LP formulation in (81). The final subsection gives the more compact formulation announced in §3.3.

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be the underlying simple graph, with _m_=|_E_|. Write _H=B<sup>T</sup>_ and take _h<sub>ve</sub>_ to denote the entry of the matrix _H_ indexed by vertex _v_ and edge _e_. Each edge represents a symbol in the codeword, and each vertex represents a parity check. If _e_={_u,v_}, then column _e_ has nonzero entries in rows _u_ and _v_ and zeros in all other rows. For each vertex _v_, write

\(\partial v=\{e\in E:h_{ve}\neq 0\},d_v=|\partial v|.\) (203)

Thus \(\partial v\) is the support of the parity check at _v_, or equivalently the set of edges that have _v_ as an endpoint. A symbol string \(\mathbf{b}\in\unknown_q^E\) has syndrome **s** precisely when

\(\sum_{e\in\partial v}h_{ve}b_e=s_v\text{for every}v\in V.\) (204)

Although Theorem 6 is stated for homological cycle codes, the proof below applies to arbitrary cycle codes ker_H_ over F_<sub>q</sub>_ with the column supports just specified. We do not require _h<sub>ue</sub>+h<sub>ve</sub>_=0 for _e_={_u,v_}. Consequently, the certified rate in Corollary 2 also applies to nonhomological cycle codes whose underlying graphs belong to the Linial-Simkin ensemble.

For fixed maximum degree _D_, the direct LP already has polynomial size in _n_=|_V_|, _m_, and _q_: each nonempty check involves at most _D_ symbols and has at most _q_<sup>_D_-1</sup> satisfying assignments. The recovery proof below uses only this formulation, with the symbol marginals _x<sub>e,a</sub>_, the local assignment probabilities \(\lambda_{v,\mathbf{b}}\), and the objective L defined in §3.3.

We first compare a competing feasible LP solution with the true error vector. For each edge, we consider the total probability that the solution’s symbol marginal assigns to values other than the true error value. We call these quantities _disagreement probabilities_. The parity checks impose inequalities on these probabilities, which we use to construct a distribution on nonbacktracking walks in _G_. A competing solution with no larger objective value would force some such walk to have at least half of its positions corrupted. Walks shorter than the girth are simple paths, so counting paths and bounding their error probabilities proves the theorem. Only after completing this recovery argument do we introduce a reformulation that removes the exponential dependence of the LP size on _D_.

## B.1 Disagreement probabilities and the LP objective

Fix an error vector **e** and its syndrome **s**=_H_**e**. Let **x**<sup>**e**</sup> be the corresponding integral feasible marginal vector, with entries \(x_{f,a}^\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{1}\{a=e_f\}\). For any other feasible marginal vector **x**, define the disagreement probabilities by

\(z_f:=1-x_{f,e_f}=\sum_{a\in\unknown_q\backslash\{e_f\}}x_{f,a},\) (205)

and put

\(T:=\{f:e_f\neq 0\},\omega_f:=1-2\mathbf{1}\{f\in T\}.\) (206)

Thus _T_ is the set of erroneous edges, and \(\omega_f\) is +1 on an uncorrupted edge and -1 on a corrupted edge. The vector **z** is nonnegative, and \(\mathbf{z}\neq 0\) whenever \(\mathbf{x}\neq\mathbf{x}^\mathbf{e}\).

Fix a vertex _v_ and sample a local assignment **b** from a distribution \(\lambda_{v,\mathbf{b}}\) witnessing feasibility of **x**. Both **b** and the restriction of **e** to \(\partial v\) satisfy the check at _v_, so

\(\sum_{f\in\partial v}h_{vf}(b_f-e_f)=0.\) (207)

These two assignments cannot differ on exactly one edge _f_ in the check support: that would give _h<sub>vf</sub>(b<sub>f</sub>-e<sub>f</sub>_)=0 with both factors nonzero in F_<sub>q</sub>_. Therefore, if \(b_f\neq e_f\), there must be another edge \(f'\in\partial v\backslash\{f\}\) on which \(b_{f^\prime}\neq e_{f^\prime}\). By local consistency, the probabilities of these disagreements are _z<sub>f</sub>_ and \(z_{f^\prime}\). A union bound gives

\(z_f\le\sum_{f^\prime\in\partial v\backslash\{f\}}z_{f^\prime}\) (208)

for every \(v\in V\) and \(f\in\partial v\). This is the only algebraic property of the checks used in the recovery argument. It uses nonzero entries within each check support, but no relation between the entries at the two endpoints of an edge. It also uses only one local assignment distribution at a time; no joint distribution on complete syndrome-consistent words is assumed.

On an uncorrupted edge, the objective difference is 1-_x_<sub>_f,_0</sub>=_z<sub>f</sub>_. On a corrupted edge, it is \(-x_{f,0}\ge-z_f\), because \(e_f\neq 0\) and \(x_{f,0}\le 1-x_{f,e_f}\). Summing these contributions gives

\(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x})-|\mathbf{e}|\ge\sum_f\omega_fz_f.\) (209)

In particular, \(\mathbf{x}\neq\mathbf{x}^\mathbf{e}\) and \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x})\le|\mathbf{e}|\) imply that **z** is nonzero, satisfies (208), and obeys \(\sum_f\omega_fz_f\le 0\). Equivalently,

\(\sum_{f:e_f\neq 0}z_f\ge\sum_{f:e_f=0}z_f.\) (210)

The comparison applies to all feasible marginal vectors, including fractional solutions and equal-cost ties.

## B.2 From disagreement probabilities to walks

A nonbacktracking walk traverses adjacent edges without immediately reversing the previous edge. We now use (208) to construct a random walk that has probability proportional to _z<sub>f</sub>_ of traversing edge _f_ at each step. This converts the objective comparison into a statement about the error locations along walks.

**Lemma 11** (Walks with prescribed edge probabilities)**.** _Let_ \(\mathbf{z}\neq 0\) _be nonnegative edge weights satisfying (208), and write_ \(Z=\sum_fz_f\)_. For every integer_ \(h\ge 1\) _there is a probability distribution on nonbacktracking walks W_=(_F_<sub>1</sub>_,...,F<sub>h</sub>_) _of h edges with_ Pr(_F<sub>i</sub>=f_)=_z<sub>f</sub>/Z for every step i. Consequently,_

\(\unknown_W\left[\sum_{i=1}^h\omega_{F_i}\right]=\frac{h}{Z}\sum_f\omega_fz_f\) (211)

_for every real edge-weight vector_ \(\unknown\)_. Repeated edges are counted with multiplicity._

_Proof._ For each vertex _v_, put \(S_v=\sum_{f\in\partial v}z_f\). The inequalities (208) say that no edge in the check support has weight greater than _S<sub>v</sub>/_2. We construct nonnegative numbers \(b_{ff^\prime}^v\), indexed by \(f,f'\in\partial v\), that are symmetric in \(f,f'\), vanish when \(f=f'\), and sum to _z<sub>f</sub>_ over \(f'\). After arrival along an edge _f_ with _z<sub>f</sub>\>_0, the ratio \(b_{ff^\prime}^v/z_f\) will be the probability of continuing along \(f'\).

If _S<sub>v</sub>\>_0, partition a circle of circumference _S<sub>v</sub>_ into consecutive half-open intervals _I<sub>f</sub>_ of lengths _z<sub>f</sub>_, and let

\(b_{ff^\prime}^v=\left|I_f\cap(I_{f^\prime}+S_v/2)\right|.\) (212)

Here addition is modulo _S<sub>v</sub>_, and the absolute-value signs denote arc length. Rotating by half the circumference preserves length and is its own inverse, so \(b_{ff^\prime}^v=b_{f^\prime f}^v\). An interval of length at most _S<sub>v</sub>/_2 is disjoint from its half-turn except possibly at endpoints, so \(b_{ff}^v=0\). The rotated intervals partition the circle, giving row sums \(\sum_{f^\prime\in\partial v}b_{ff^\prime}^v=|I_f|=z_f\). Set _b<sup>v</sup>_=0 when _S<sub>v</sub>_=0.

Choose the first directed edge from the following distribution on both directions of each edge with _z<sub>f</sub>\>_0:

\(\pi(u,v)=\frac{z_{\{u,v\}}}{2Z}.\) (213)

After traversing _f_={_u,v_} towards _v_, choose the next edge \(f'=\{v,w\}\) with probability \(b_{ff^\prime}^v/z_f\). The row sums make this a Markov chain, and the zero diagonal prohibits immediate reversal. For each directed edge (_v,w_), its incoming probability under \(\pi\) is

\(\sum_{u:\{u,v\}\in E}\frac{z_{\{u,v\}}}{2Z}\frac{b_{\{u,v\},\{v,w\}}^v}{z_{\{u,v\}}}=\frac{z_{\{v,w\}}}{2Z}=\pi(v,w),\) (214)

where terms with zero weight are omitted. Thus \(\pi\) is _stationary_: the distribution on directed edges is unchanged after a step. At every step, the probability of traversing the undirected edge _f_ is therefore _z<sub>f</sub>/Z_. Summing the expected edge weights over the _h_ steps proves (211).

**Lemma 12** (A sufficient condition for unique LP recovery)**.** _Fix_ \(h\ge 1\)_. If every nonbacktracking walk of h edges has strictly fewer than h/_2 _erroneous positions, counting multiplicity, then_ **x**<sup>**e**</sup> _is the unique optimal marginal vector of the LP. In particular the LP decoder returns_ **e**.

_Proof._ A walk’s total weight is _h_ minus twice its number of erroneous positions, so the hypothesis makes every such weight strictly positive. If a distinct feasible marginal vector **x** satisfied \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x})\le|\mathbf{e}|\), then (209) and Lemma 11 would give a distribution on these walks with nonpositive expected weight, a contradiction.

This condition is sufficient, not necessary: the existence of a walk with at least half its positions corrupted does not by itself imply a decoding failure. The argument rules out both integral and fractional competitors, including equal-cost ties, and depends only on the error locations.

## B.3 Probability of a bad path

_Proof of Theorem 6._ If _h\<g<sub>G</sub>_, every nonbacktracking walk of _h_ edges is a simple path: a first repeated vertex would yield a cycle of length at most _h_. There are at most 2_m(D_-1)<sup>_h_-1</sup> oriented such paths, because the first edge has 2_m_ orientations and each subsequent step has at most _D_-1 choices.

For a fixed path, let _X_ count its erroneous positions. Under independent symbol errors, _X_ has the Bin(_h,p_) distribution. For _p\<_1/2, Markov’s inequality with _s_=(1-_p)/p\>_1 yields

\(Pr\{X\ge h/2\}\le s^{-h/2}(1-p+ps)^h=\left[2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\right]^h.\) (215)

Lemma 12 and a union bound prove (83). This argument bounds an event depending only on the support, so it permits arbitrary nonzero values at corrupted positions.

For the fixed-weight assertion, put \(\rho=t/m\). If _t_=0 the LP has the zero word as its unique optimal marginal vector. Otherwise, for a uniformly chosen _t_-subset of edges and \(s\ge 1\), expansion of _s<sup>X</sup>_ gives

\(\unknown s^X=\sum_{j=0}^h\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{j}(s-1)^j\frac{(t)_j}{(m)_j}\le(1-\rho+\rho s)^h.\) (216)

Here \((a)_j=a(a-1)\cdots(a-j+1)\), with (_t)<sub>j</sub>_=0 for _j\>t_, and \((t)_j/(m)_j\le(t/m)^j\). Applying (215) with \(\rho\) in place of _p_ proves the same bound because \(\rho\le p<1/2\) and \(2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\) is increasing on \[0,1/2\].

For independent noise at any fixed positive rate in Corollary 2, the error weight is _pm+o(m_) with probability tending to one. The fixed-weight version proves the linear-error statement without using this concentration step. Neither version gives correction of all adversarial supports of linear size.

### Recovery after a one-coordinate change.

Changing one coordinate can increase the number of corrupted positions on a simple path by at most one. Hence, if every simple path of _h\<g<sub>G</sub>_ edges contains fewer than _h/_2-1 corrupted positions, then every word at Hamming distance at most one from the error satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 12. Each such word is therefore uniquely LP-recoverable from its own syndrome. With _s_=(1-_p)/p_, the tail estimate (215) becomes

\(Pr\{X\ge h/2-1\}\le s^{1-h/2}(1-p+ps)^h=\frac{1-p}{p}\left[2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\right]^h.\) (217)

For a uniformly chosen support of size \(t\le pm\), use (216) with the same _s_ and \(t/m\le p\). A union bound proves (84) in both cases. The bound is uniform over all nonzero values, including replacements introduced by the one-coordinate change.

## B.4 An equivalent LP with polynomial dependence on the degree

The recovery proof is complete. We now establish the stronger size bound stated in §3.3. A check involving \(d_v\ge 1\) symbols has exactly _q_<sup>_d<sub>v</sub>_-1</sup> satisfying assignments: the first _d<sub>v</sub>_-1 symbol values can be chosen freely, and the check uniquely determines the last value because its coefficient is nonzero. After omitting empty checks, the direct LP therefore has

\(mq+\sum_{v:d_v>0}q^{d_v-1}\le mq+nq^{D-1}\) (218)

variables. Its number of constraints and their encoding size are also polynomial in _n_, _m_, and _q_ for fixed _D_, and all scalar coefficients are \(0,\pm 1\). Thus the direct formulation already admits polynomial- time LP optimization in that setting. The construction below instead has _O(mq_<sup>2</sup>) variables and constraints, hence _O(nDq_<sup>2</sup>) for maximum degree _D_. Its size has no exponential dependence on _D_.

## Representing a parity check by a layered graph.

Fix a syndrome \(\mathbf{s}\in\mathrm{im}H\). For each nonempty check, we construct a separate auxiliary directed graph, called a _trellis_. Its nodes are arranged in successive layers, and its directed edges go from one layer to the next. These nodes are not vertices of _G_: they record running sums as the symbols in one check are assigned values.

Fix a vertex _v_ with _d<sub>v</sub>\>_0, and order the edges in its parity-check support as \(\partial v=\{e_1,\dots,e_{d_v}\}\). At layer _i_=0_,...,d<sub>v</sub>_, include one node (_i,z_) for each \(z\in\unknown_q\). The node records the weighted partial sum \(z=\sum_{j=1}^ih_{ve_j}b_{e_j}\). Assigning the next symbol value _b<sub>e<sub>i</sub></sub>=a_ is represented by the directed edge

\((i-1,z)\rightarrow(i,z+h_{ve_i}a),\text{labelled}a.\) (219)

We include this edge for every _i_=1_,...,d<sub>v</sub>_ and \(z,a\in\unknown_q\). Starting at (0,0), each sequence of symbol values determines exactly one path. The assignment satisfies the check precisely when that path ends at (_d<sub>v</sub>,s<sub>v</sub>_). Different partial assignments with the same weighted sum reach the same node; the graph need not store them separately.

## A binary example.

For the check _b_<sub>1</sub>+_b_<sub>2</sub>+_b_<sub>3</sub>=0 over \(\unknown_2\), the state at layer _i_ is the sum of the first _i_ symbols modulo two. Choosing 0 preserves the sum, whereas choosing 1 changes it to the other value. The full trellis has eight nodes and twelve directed edges, as shown in Fig. 2. The four paths from (0,0) to (3,0) represent exactly the satisfying assignments 000, 011, 101, and 110. For example, the assignments 000 and 110 both reach (2,0) after two steps and use the same final edge. Their earlier choices are recorded by their paths, not by separate copies of the node (2,0).

## From assignment probabilities to flows.

A probability distribution over satisfying assignments is a probability distribution over paths from (0,0) to (_d<sub>v</sub>,s<sub>v</sub>_). Send each path’s probability along its directed edges. The resulting nonnegative edge flows have total supply one at (0,0), total demand one at (_d<sub>v</sub>,s<sub>v</sub>_), and flow conservation at all other nodes, with zero supply or demand elsewhere. Conversely, any flow obeying these constraints in this acyclic graph decomposes into a convex combination of such paths, hence into a distribution over satisfying assignments.

Let _f<sub>v,i,z,a</sub>_ be the flow on the edge labelled _a_ from (_i_-1_,z_). The total flow choosing _a_ for symbol _e<sub>i</sub>_ must equal its marginal:

\(x_{e_i,a}=\sum_{z\in\unknown_q}f_{v,i,z,a}.\) (220)

Use the same variables _x<sub>e,a</sub>_ in the trellises for both endpoints of _e_, and keep the objective L(**x**) unchanged. The two formulations then have exactly the same feasible symbol marginals, and therefore the same optimal marginal vectors. The reformulation neither tightens nor weakens the LP relaxation, so all recovery guarantees proved above apply to it. A vertex with _d<sub>v</sub>_=0 imposes only _s<sub>v</sub>_=0 and can be omitted because the syndrome is valid.

## Size and complexity.

Each nonempty check uses _d<sub>v</sub>q_<sup>2</sup> directed edges and _O(d<sub>v</sub>q_) node constraints. Since \(\sum_vd_v=2m\le nD\), including the shared symbol marginals and their consistency<tbc>

<tbc>constraints gives _O(mq_<sup>2</sup>) variables and constraints in total. Each flow variable occurs in only two node equations and one marginal equation, so the number of nonzero scalar coefficients is also _O(mq_<sup>2</sup>). The field entries _h<sub>ve</sub>_ determine which nodes a directed edge connects; the real-valued LP constraints themselves have coefficients \(0,\pm 1\), as does the nonconstant part of the objective. Rational LP optimization thus takes time polynomial in _n_, _q_, and _D_. A fixed lexicographic rule on the symbol marginals can be implemented by a polynomial number of further LP optimizations, making the decoder deterministic in either formulation. This removes the exponential degree dependence in the implementation; it does not change the parameter regimes of the recovery results.
